svg.text: TO SHOW
exactly 15 numbers in 1 ≤ x ≤ 100 need four squares
By Legendre’s three-square theorem these are precisely the numbers of the form 4ᵃ(8b + 7).
Counting them is then a two-case split on a, since a = 2 already forces the number above 100.
THE COUNT, BY CASES ON a
a = 0: 8b + 7 ≤ 100 means b ≤ 11, giving twelve numbers
a = 1: 4(8b + 7) ≤ 100 means 8b + 7 ≤ 25, so 8b + 7 ∈ {7, 15, 23}, giving three numbers
a ≥ 2 needs 16(8b + 7) ≤ 100, i.e. 8b + 7 ≤ 6, which is impossible. Total: 12 + 3 = 15. ■
THE FIFTEEN, IN PLACE
red:
twelve of them,
one every eight
amber:
three of them,
one every 32
grey:
three squares
or fewer suffice
WHY THE TWO SHAPES, AND NOTHING ELSE
Squares are 0, 1 or 4 mod 8, and three of them can never total 7 mod 8 — that rules out every 8b + 7.
For the factor 4ᵃ: squares are 0 or 1 mod 4, so a² + b² + c² ≡ 0 (mod 4) forces all three to be even.
Halving each shows that if 4n is a sum of three squares then so is n — and conversely. So the property
passes up and down the chain n, 4n, 16n, … unchanged.
28, 60 and 92 are exactly 4 times the first three red entries 7, 15 and 23 — visible as the amber cells in the grid.
CHECKS
Computing the minimum number of squares directly for every n from 1 to 100 returns exactly this list of
fifteen, matching the Legendre form with no discrepancy.
The density is 15/100 = 15%, close to the asymptotic value 1/8 + 1/32 + 1/128 + ⋯ = 1/6 ≈ 16.7%.
The smallest entry is 7 and the second is 15 — the number treated by hand in the previous problem.
